overview: The DISRUPT Act focuses on the growing cooperation among China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, which the bill describes as the leading adversaries of the United States. It declares a U.S. policy of disrupting the most dangerous parts of that cooperation, using tools like the threat of sanctions and export controls and sharing information with allies. Within 60 days, the State, Defense, Treasury, and Commerce departments, the Director of National Intelligence, and the CIA would each set up a task force on this 'adversary alignment' and report on how their agencies should adapt, with the task force heads meeting every quarter. The intelligence community would have to send a classified report on how these countries cooperate and the risks that creates, and the State and Defense secretaries would have to deliver a classified strategy, including plans to build up munitions stockpiles, produce weapons jointly with allies, and modernize military war-planning tools. As of June 18, 2025, a Senate committee had approved it and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say these four countries increasingly share weapons, technology, and ways around sanctions, and that the U.S. government needs a coordinated plan across agencies to prepare for the possibility of facing more than one of them at once.
against: Critics say the bill creates six new task forces and several reports that may duplicate existing work, and that treating the four countries as a single bloc could push them closer together rather than apart.
